blocks.text: Many kinds of bacteria have flagella, which enable them to move. The secondary function of flagella is to detect and respond to chemical signals. The bacteria which do not possess flagella are called atrichous. The bacteria with single polar flagellum are called monotrichous. The bacteria with a tuft of flagella at one pole are called lophotrichous. The bacteria with flagella at each of two poles are called amphitrichous. The bacteria with flagella surrounding the whole cell are called peritrichous (Figure 2.7).

blocks.alt: Five rod-shaped cells, each named inside: Atrichous with no flagella; Monotrichous with one flagellum at one pole; Lophotrichous with a tuft of flagella at one pole; Amphitrichous with a flagellum at each of the two poles; Peritrichous with flagella all round the cell.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.7: The different arrangements of bacterial flagella (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.7).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 2.7 swaps two drawings: its 'Lophotrichous' cell has one flagellum at each pole and its 'Amphitrichous' cell has a tuft at one pole. As the book's own text says, lophotrichous is a tuft of flagella at one pole and amphitrichous is flagella at both poles, as drawn above.
